sources.citation: Vermeir, Tessa. 2024. Analyses lexicales et phonologiques des langues A80 avec un focus sur le sso. These de doctorat. 227 pp. (HAL tel-05296611)
sources.note: Njyem appears only as lexical data (LA80 database, from Beavon & Beavon 2005 lexicon). Its sec. 3.3.1 'Accentuation' (p.75) describes Sso (A82), not Njyem: non-distinctive slight stress on the first syllable of the base. Nothing on Njyem stress.

sources.citation: Beavon, Keith H. 2017. An Introduction to the Phonology and Grammar of Njyem. Yaounde: SIL. 100 pp. (SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 84927; posted on webonary.org/njyem as two PDFs). Supersedes the unpublished Beavon 2005/2006 ms. 'A phonology of Njyem' (Glottolog 306048).
sources.note: Ch.2 Phonology (pp.7-74): segmental phonology by stem position, syllable types, then sec. 2.2 'Suprasegmental Phonology' (p.25 ff.) entirely on tone (H, L, status of mid, tone rules, boundary tones). The only mention of stress is incidental (p.25): pitch is lexically contrastive and 'There is no constraint such as stress or consonant feature that would enable one to guess the pitch.' No section on stress/accent and no statement of where stress falls; no other prominence vocabulary (penult, intensity, rhythm) anywhere.

sources.note: Ch.4 sec. 2.5 'Njem (A84)', pp.246-258: second-hand synthesis of Beavon (2005) and Akumbu (2006, 2009) -- noun classes, syllable types, vowels, consonants, 2.5.5 Tons (two registers H/B; mid is phonetic; polar tone), recap tables 66-67. The word 'accent' does not occur in the Njem section (nor elsewhere in the thesis). Silent on stress.

sources.citation: Akumbu, Pius Wuchu. 2012 [2006]. Njem Tonology. SIL e-Books 45. Dallas: SIL International. 309 pp. (= PhD thesis, Universite de Yaounde I, defended 19 Jan 2007; Glottolog 161938; SIL archives 51669; HAL tel-03692270).
sources.note: Ch.2 'Segmental phonology': consonants by root position, 10 vowels + length, 2.3 Tones (pp.53-55: two underlying tones H/L, contours = sequences, TBU = syllable), 2.4 canonical syllable structure, features, processes; ch.4-5 tone in nouns/verbs (RTT). No section or statement on word stress/accent. Only incidental uses: p.46 generic 'vowels.. carry such intonational features as stress and pitch'; pp.69-70 considers and rejects treating the class 6 prefix meN- as 'accented' to explain devoicing ('prefixes are not usually accented').

sources.note: Content unseen (title only). An SIL Cameroon orthography statement for Njyem necessarily fixes tone-marking conventions; Beavon 2017 (a work listed here, sec. 2.2) describes the conventions actually used (acute/grave for H/L, macron for the mid generated by the polar suffix on high-tone verbs), which presumably follow this orthography ms. No analytic tone statement expected beyond the inventory of written tones.

sources.note: Secondhand (Akumbu 2006: 11, sec. 1.6): 'In (2000), Akumbu wrote Tone in Njem nouns (ms). He argues for the existence of four underlying tonal melodies: H, L, LH and HL on Njem nouns and identifies three sets of associative constructions based on the behaviour of tones in each set.' Akumbu 2006: ch. 4 also cites 'Akumbu 2000: 1' for the two level tones High and Low of noun roots. Superseded by Akumbu 2006 ch. 4 and Akumbu 2009 (a work listed here/8).
